problem: Source says the lawyers 'secretly' oppose; 'quietly' drops the covert sense.
replacement: The more we reflect on everything that happens in the United States, the more we will be persuaded that lawyers as a body form the most powerful counterpoise to the democratic element, if not the only one. In that country we see how well the legal profession is suited, by its strengths and even by its defects, to neutralize the vices inherent in popular government. When the American people is intoxicated by passion or swept away by the impetuosity of its ideas, it is checked and stopped by the almost invisible influence of its legal counselors. These counselors secretly set their aristocratic inclinations against its democratic instincts, their superstitious attachment to what is old against its love of novelty, their narrow views against its immense designs, and their habitual delay against its ardent impatience.

I consider this one of the chief causes of the maintenance of republican institutions in the United States. In cities it is impossible to prevent people from acting in concert and stirring one another into sudden and passionate resolutions. replacement: In Europe we often carry the ideas and habits of private life into public affairs. Since we pass at once from the family circle to the government of the state, we can often be heard discussing the great interests of society in the same way we talk with our friends. The Americans, on the other hand, carry the habits of public life over into their private customs. In their country the jury system is brought into the games of schoolboys, and parliamentary rules are followed in arranging a feast.

replacement: I have observed that the maintenance of democratic institutions in the United States is due to the circumstances, the laws, and the customs of that country. *l Most Europeans know only the first of these three causes, and they tend to give it an overriding importance that it does not really have.

problem: Thesis paragraph on moeurs still says 'manners' throughout (STYLE-NOTE: customs); also 'very much subordinate' is clumsy.
replacement: The customs of the Americans of the United States are, then, the real reason why that people alone, among the American nations, can sustain a democratic government. It is the influence of customs that produces the different degrees of order and prosperity that can be seen in the several Anglo-American democracies. Europe, therefore, exaggerates what the geographical position of a country can do for the durability of democratic institutions. It gives too much weight to legislation and too little to customs. These three great causes no doubt help to regulate and direct the American democracy. But if I had to rank them in their proper order, I would say that physical circumstances count for less than the laws, and the laws are greatly subordinate to the customs of the people. I am convinced that the most favorable situation and the best possible laws cannot sustain a constitution against the customs of a country, while customs can turn even the most unfavorable situations and the worst laws to some advantage. The importance of customs is a common truth to which study and experience keep bringing us back. It may be regarded as the central point in the range of human observation, and the place where all inquiry finally ends. I insist on this point so seriously that, if I have failed to make the reader feel the great influence I attribute to the practical experience, the habits, the opinions, in short the customs of the Americans, on the survival of their institutions, then I have failed in the main object of my work.

problem: Manners (moeurs) should be customs per STYLE-NOTE.
replacement: First, it seems to me that we must carefully distinguish the institutions of the United States from democratic institutions in general. When I think about Europe, with its mighty nations, populous cities, and formidable armies, and with the complexity of its politics, I cannot suppose that even the Anglo-Americans could live in our hemisphere with their ideas, their religion, and their customs and not alter their laws considerably. But we can imagine a democratic nation organized differently from the American people. It is not impossible to conceive of a government truly founded on the will of the majority, in which the majority nevertheless holds back its natural leaning toward equality. For the sake of order and stability in the state, it would consent to give a family or an individual all the prerogatives of the executive. A democratic society might exist in which the forces of the nation were more centralized than they are in the United States. The people would then have a less direct and less irresistible influence on public affairs, and yet every citizen, invested with certain rights, would still take part, within his own sphere, in running the government. What I observed among the Anglo-Americans leads me to believe that democratic institutions of this kind, if prudently introduced so that they gradually blend with the habits and mingle with the opinions of the people, might survive in other countries besides America. If the laws of the United States were the only democratic laws one could imagine, or the most perfect, I would admit that their success proves nothing about the success of democratic institutions in general in a country less favored by nature. But the laws of America seem to me defective in several ways, and I can easily imagine others of the same general kind. So the particular advantages of that country do not prove that democratic institutions cannot succeed in a nation less favored by circumstances, if it is ruled by better laws.

problem: Defined term: 'manners and laws' (moeurs) must be 'customs' per STYLE-NOTE.
replacement: The customs and laws of the Americans are not the only ones that may suit a democratic people. But the Americans have shown that it would be wrong to despair of regulating democracy with the help of customs and laws. Suppose other nations take this general and fruitful idea from the Americans, without meaning to copy the particular way they have applied it. Suppose they try to prepare themselves for the social condition that Providence seems to impose on the generations of this age, and so to escape the despotism or the anarchy that threatens them. What reason is there to suppose that their efforts would fail? The organization and establishment of democracy in Christendom is the great political problem of the time. The Americans, unquestionably, have not solved this problem, but they supply useful data to those who undertake the task.

When the war broke out between ourselves and the English in 1810, I saw this young man again; he was serving in our army, at the head of the warriors of his tribe, for the Indians were admitted among the ranks of the Americans, upon condition that they would abstain from their horrible custom of scalping their victims. On the evening of the battle of . . ., C. came and sat himself down by the fire of our bivouac. I asked him what had been his fortune that day: he related his exploits; and growing warm and animated by the recollection of them, he concluded by suddenly opening the breast of his coat, saying, ‘You must not betray me — see here!’ And I actually beheld,” said the Major, “between his body and his shirt, the skin and hair of an English head, still dripping with gore.”]
